title: Joshua 4:15–24
context: The chapter closes the crossing account. At the LORD’s word Joshua commands the priests to come up out of the Jordan, and as soon as their feet touch dry ground the river returns to flood stage. The narrator dates the event to the tenth day of the first month, the day Israel was to set aside the Passover lamb according to Exodus 12:3, and Israel camps at Gilgal, where the Passover will be kept in 5:10. Joshua sets up the twelve stones at Gilgal and repeats the instruction to explain them to children: God dried up the Jordan as he dried up the Red Sea, so that all the peoples of the earth would know the LORD’s hand is mighty and Israel would fear him forever. Both traditions read this as shared ground: God acts in history, links his later works to his earlier ones, and intends his saving deeds to be remembered, taught, and proclaimed beyond Israel. Exodus and baptismal typology may be noted, but the text itself focuses on memory, worship, and the fear of the LORD.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Joshua, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD speaks to Joshua again as the narrative returns to the priests still standing in the riverbed. The final step of the crossing waits on God’s word just as the first did.

Arminian readers note that God directs every stage of his people’s journey, including when to move on. The relationship between God and Joshua remains personal and responsive, with God speaking and Joshua listening and acting.
verses.reformedNotes:
This verse resumes the account of the priests in the river, and the narrative’s careful structure shows that God governs both the beginning and the end of the miracle.

Reformed readers stress that God’s word sets the timing of every step. Both traditions agree that the priests do not leave the river on their own initiative but wait for God’s command through Joshua.

verses.text: “Command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, that they come up out of the Jordan.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Joshua to command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant to come up out of the Jordan. The priests have held their place until now, and only God’s word releases them.

Arminian readers see patience and obedience in the priests’ waiting. They stay at their post until God says the work is done, a picture of faithful service that does not quit early.
verses.reformedNotes:
The command for the priests to come up shows that God determines when his work is complete and when his servants may leave their post.

Reformed readers emphasize God’s ordering of every detail of the event. Both traditions agree that the verse displays God’s authority over the timing of his saving work and the faithful service of those who carry the ark.

verses.text: Joshua therefore commanded the priests, saying, “Come up out of the Jordan!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua commands the priests, “Come up out of the Jordan!” The command passes exactly from God to Joshua to the priests, with no addition or delay.

Arminian readers note Joshua’s prompt faithfulness in relaying God’s word. The leader does not improvise but speaks what God has said, and the people are called to respond to that word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joshua’s command repeats God’s instruction exactly, showing that his authority depends on faithfully passing on God’s word.

Reformed readers stress that God’s servants lead best when they speak only what God has commanded. Both traditions agree that the verse models faithful mediation of God’s word and prepares for the river’s return.

verses.text: When the priests who bore the ark of the LORD’s covenant had come up out of the middle of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests’ feet had been lifted up to the dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place, and went over all its banks, as before.
verses.arminianNotes:
As soon as the soles of the priests’ feet are lifted onto dry ground, the waters of the Jordan return and flood its banks as before. The river’s return confirms that its stopping was tied to the ark’s presence.

Arminian readers see the timing as a clear sign that God acted in response to his own word and his people’s obedience. The return of the flood makes the miracle unmistakable.
verses.reformedNotes:
The waters return exactly when the priests leave the riverbed, which shows that the stopping of the river was not coincidental but the deliberate work of God.

Reformed readers emphasize God’s precise control over creation for his people’s sake. Both traditions agree that the verse frames the miracle, with the waters stopping at the priests’ first step and returning at their last.

verses.text: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and encamped in Gilgal, on the east border of Jericho.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people come up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month and camp at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho. The date matches the day Israel was to set aside the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:3), and the Passover follows in 5:10.

Arminian readers note that God brings his people into the land at a time that recalls their deliverance from Egypt. Their faith is anchored in a history of God’s saving acts.
verses.reformedNotes:
The date links the crossing to the Passover calendar and roughly forty years after the exodus, so the new generation enters the land in step with the story of redemption that began in Egypt.

Reformed readers see God’s providence in the timing, joining the exodus and the entry into the land as parts of one unfolding plan. Both traditions agree that the date ties the crossing closely to Passover and to God’s faithfulness over many years.

verses.text: Joshua set up those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, in Gilgal.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua sets up at Gilgal the twelve stones that were taken out of the Jordan. The memorial now stands at Israel’s first camp in the land.

Arminian readers note that the memorial is placed where the people will live and gather, so it will be seen and asked about. Remembering God’s acts is built into the life of the community rather than left to chance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Gilgal becomes an important base in the following chapters, so placing the stones there puts the memorial at the heart of Israel’s early life in the land.

Reformed readers stress that God provides lasting signs of his works where his people worship and gather. Both traditions agree that the memorial at Gilgal anchors Israel’s identity in what God did at the Jordan.

verses.text: He spoke to the children of Israel, saying, “When your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, ‘What do these stones mean?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua tells the people that when children ask their fathers in time to come, “What do these stones mean?” they must answer. The instruction repeats and reinforces 4:6.

Arminian readers stress the responsibility of parents to explain God’s works to their children. Each generation needs to hear the story in a way that invites its own faith and obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repetition of the children’s question emphasizes that teaching the next generation is central to the purpose of the memorial.

Reformed readers stress the covenant family, in which parents explain God’s promises and works to their children as part of ordinary life. Both traditions agree that the verse calls parents to tell the next generation what God has done.

verses.text: Then you shall let your children know, saying, ‘Israel came over this Jordan on dry land.
verses.arminianNotes:
The answer begins simply: “Israel came over this Jordan on dry land.” The story is told plainly enough for a child to grasp and remember.

Arminian readers note that the heart of the testimony is a clear account of what God did. Faith is passed on through simple, faithful storytelling that invites the hearer to trust the God who acted.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase “on dry land” echoes the Red Sea account and identifies the crossing as another great act of deliverance.

Reformed readers stress that the testimony centers on God’s act rather than on Israel’s effort. Both traditions agree that the verse gives parents a clear, God-centered summary of the event to pass on.

verses.text: For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan from before you until you had crossed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up from before us, until we had crossed over,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD dried up the Jordan until Israel crossed, “as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea.” The verse explicitly links the two crossings, and the shift from “you” to “us” draws the speakers into the earlier story.

Arminian readers note that each generation is invited to see itself within the history of God’s saving acts. The New Testament draws on the Red Sea crossing as a pattern for Christian baptism (compare 1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and some Arminian readers extend that pattern to the Jordan.
verses.reformedNotes:
The explicit link to the Red Sea shows that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt is the same God who brings them into the land, so the exodus and the conquest belong to one story of redemption.

Reformed readers often see in both crossings a pattern fulfilled in Christ and signified in baptism, while respecting the text’s own focus on God’s historical acts. Both traditions agree that the verse joins past and present deliverance in a single confession of God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD’s hand is mighty, and that you may fear the LORD your God forever.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The purpose of God’s act is twofold: “that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD’s hand is mighty,” and that Israel “may fear the LORD your God forever.” The memorial looks outward to the nations and inward to Israel’s worship.

Arminian readers stress the outward reach of God’s act: his power is shown so that the nations may know him. Israel’s reverent fear is the right response, renewed in each generation.
verses.reformedNotes:
God’s saving acts serve his glory among the nations and the lasting reverence of his people, and both purposes are named here.

Reformed readers emphasize that God’s glory is the ultimate goal of his works, and that the fear of the LORD is the fitting response of a redeemed people. Both traditions agree that the verse shows God’s concern for the nations and his desire for his people’s enduring reverence.
